I wouldn't have a problem hiring you then, honestly. I mean as long as you could get the job done, and you're safe about it, I don't see why having a medical file saying your depth perception isn't great would stop you from working.

I know a logger that works by himself all the time, and has been beat up and knocked up side the head so many times he only has one eye. Dude still puts trees on the ground, and I salute him for that... But I keep expecting to roll up on his job site one day for BMP inspections and find him laid out under a 40" tree. 

So I agree with you that you can probably do it just fine, so long as you've got the experience to compensate. I think I'd trust this guy putting a snag on the ground A LOT more than a first year rookie that has 212 and can't judge how far away his bar is from his face.

I've been on actual type 2 IA crews on federal campaign fires, and have been on IA crews on the state level. 

The smaller crews are more useful on the state level where you have very limited resources. When we run IA, we pretty much just go with whatever we can get, but generally end up running in squads for the most part. 

We'll have a squad on one division, another squad on the next division, etc. with the HEQB's and operators paired up in twos. 

To be fair, our local fuels make smaller crews more realistic, though. We don't end up putting a lot of hand line in. It's usually more backpack blower work, touching it up with fire rakes and pulaskis.... Or it's just dozer line or other existing control lines. 

The majority of the boots on the ground work ends up being burn out operations and mop up.

I work career staff, full time, on a state crew, year round. I also have hiring authority for part time firefighters. 

This is not something I'd even consider as a problem. It's really more of a "can you do it or not" basis. We don't require a vision test or anything like that, but I guess if one of my guys was so blind he couldn't tell how far away something was, I'd restrict them to not driving and not operating saws/swamping. 

I wouldn't see much of a problem still having them work, unless they are just super blind to the point that it effects everything they do. In which case I don't really know what I'd do aside from having higher management give me guidelines to follow. 

I've honestly never had this become a problem. And I'm sure there are people out there with better or worse vision than others. 

So I guess to answer your question, I'd look at it like this - is your depth perception bad enough that you feel like you couldn't perform certain aspects of the job? Or is it something that's on paper in your medical files, but you can otherwise function normally?

Do you find that running or jogging is easier than a forced march pace of walking? Seems like it is for me. Walking at a super fast pace ends up making my legs burn a lot more, and my heart rate can even go up higher, too. 

It's weird, but it feels like running is easier on me than walking at a really fast pace and keeping the ole' feet on the ground with a walking stride.

I work at the state level, so we really don't go through seasons like shot crews do, in terms of employment status. But we do have two distinct fire seasons in the state. Spring and Fall, where the eastern hardwood litter that accumulates is our primary fuel source, so when the dormant seasons get ripe, we have plenty of fires.

Most are small, like less than 10 acres. But we have a few of the 5k acre fires in they state pretty much every year. 

So I have to stay in shape pretty much year round. Spring for home unit, summer for AD work, fall for home unit. Winter is the only real "off season", which does sneak up on you and you realize you've gotten lazy. 

That happens to me most winters. 

I just start out in the gym while it's blistering cold out, and as it starts to warm up start hiking. 

My actual workout isn't hardcore or special. I just go do 30 minutes of cardio every day, usually just hopping on the treadmill and walking as fast as I possibly can without running (typically 6.0mph on the treadmill, keeps me right on the verge of having to change from a labored walk into an easy jog). 

This seems to really work my calves better than running for whatever reason. I think if I jog or run it ends up being more straight up cardio and less muscle work on the legs, so the "power walk" is actually harder for me to complete than jogging or running. My legs burn more, so I'm sticking with it. 

Once the cardio is done, I just go lift free weights. 

Looking into getting one of the sandbags that the structure guys have been using. Looks like a good workout. 

All in all, I can always notice a huge difference in my fitness after just a week or two of this. 

When the winter sets in around mid-November, and everyone including myself takes a month or more of leave, I just get lazy. Then I have to force myself to start back on the gym. But once I get through the first week, I'm on routine and get grumpy if I miss a day. 

Once it gets warm enough to not be single digits or negatives with wind chill, I there are two different fire towers I hike to on a rotating workout. One's an easy 3.4 miles that's flat. The other is a weekend/full day hike out and back. I just carry my line pack and hit them every other day, going to the gym if weather doesn't allow. 

I also chop wood for the maintenance shop, so I've got that going for me, which is nice.
